newsitem.title: UK: Algerian bomb suspect still in custody in Britain.
newsitem.headline: Algerian bomb suspect still in custody in Britain.

text.p: An Algerian accused by Paris of involvement in a bombing campaign in France last year is still being held in a London prison pending his appeal against deportation from Britain.
A police spokeswoman said on Wednesday a date for the appeal in London's High Court by Rachid Ramda has yet to be set. He was being held in Belmarsh high-security prison in east London.

Police sources said there was a "long line" of people waiting for appeals to be heard and many had been in prison on remand longer than Ramda. Police arrested Ramda in London on November 5, 1995, under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
In June a British magistrate ordered Ramda, 26, to be extradited to France where he faces 23 charges linked to a militant Islamic bombing campaign. Ramda launched an appeal.

A bomb tore through a Paris train on Tuesday, killing two people. It bore the hallmarks of last year's bombings and caused French anti-terrorism investigators to wonder whether they had brushed off threats from Algerian extremists too quickly.

A lawyer for the French government told the court in June Ramda was an influential member of Algeria's Armed Islamic Group (GIA). Ramda faces charges including conspiracy to murder and to cause explosions likely to endanger life and damage property.
GIA claimed responsibility for the 1995 bombs, accusing France of siding with Algeria's military government in a war against Moslem fundamentalists.

Ramda's lawyer said they would contest the extradition order "because the accusations against him are not made in good faith". She said if Ramda was returned to France he would be "prejudiced at the trial" due to race, nationality, political and religious opinions.

London is home to numerous exile groups and opposition newspapers from around the world. Critics have accused the British government of not doing enough to stop an active minority from fomenting trouble.
One of the reasons that London attracts exiled activists is that under British laws, refugees do not have to give up being politically active when claiming asylum.

Government attempts to crack down on those it feels are abusing British hospitality suffered a setback in March when Home Secretary Michael Howard failed in a bid to deport fundamentalist Islamic dissident Mohammed al-Masari.
Masari's outspoken attacks on the Saudi royal family strained relations with Riyadh and caused British businesses to complain about losing lucrative contracts.
In November government sources said Britain was preparing a law that would allow authorities to jail foreign dissidents who plotted against other countries.
The sources said dissidents conspiring to overthrow foreign governments or to cause "substantive acts" abroad could face imprisonment if the new law was passed.
